title: Delegate access
intro: OAuth lets a client obtain delegated access. The authorization server issues tokens that a resource API can validate.
takeaway: OAuth is an access-delegation protocol. PKCE protects one part of an authorization-code flow; it is not a universal permission check.

beats.text: A client needs access to an API. An authorization server handles the grant.
The user authorizes access in a browser. The client receives an authorization code.
The client exchanges the code for tokens. The server validates the exchange.
A token accompanies an API request. The API still checks access.

title: Create a verifier
intro: For each authorization attempt, the client creates a fresh unpredictable verifier and retains it for that attempt. S256 derives a challenge from it.
takeaway: The verifier is a secret for this transaction. A later login needs a different verifier and separate storage.

beats.text: Start a new authorization attempt. Create a fresh unpredictable verifier.
Keep that verifier with attempt A. It will be needed at token exchange.
Derive its S256 challenge. The challenge is a transformed value.
Send the challenge first. Keep the verifier for the later exchange.

title: Bind code and challenge
intro: The client sends its challenge with the authorization request. After authorization, the server issues a code bound to that challenge.
takeaway: The first leg sends the challenge, not the verifier. Normal OAuth request validation and user authorization still apply.

beats.text: The client has challenge A. Its verifier remains with the client.
Send challenge A for authorization. The server records it for this attempt.
After authorization, issue code A. The server binds it to challenge A.
A code alone is not the full proof. The exchange must match the challenge.

title: Prove the verifier matches
intro: The client submits the authorization code and the original verifier. The authorization server derives a challenge from the verifier and compares it with the saved value.
takeaway: A matching PKCE check allows the rest of token validation to proceed. A mismatch must fail; it should not disable the protection.

beats.text: Submit code A with verifier A. The server has its saved challenge.
Derive S256 from the submitted verifier. Compare it with saved challenge A.
A matching proof passes this check. Other OAuth checks must also pass.
Then tokens may be issued. The code and proof belong together.

title: Separate login attempts
intro: Two logins overlap. If B overwrites a global verifier, exchanging code A with verifier B fails. Store each verifier with its own transaction.
takeaway: Repair transaction-specific storage and start a fresh login. Do not disable PKCE or repeatedly send mismatched credentials.

beats.text: Attempt A owns code A and verifier A. Attempt B needs its own stored verifier.
A shared variable is overwritten by B. Code A is now paired with verifier B.
The server checks the mismatched proof. It must reject this token exchange.
Keep verifier storage per transaction. Repair the client; start a fresh login.
